Highlights 

  • Utah’s Legislative Session Closes with Three More Bills Headed to the Governor: SB 150 (health), HB 276 (genAI), and HB 450 (privacy/ADMT) head to the Governor’s desk while chatbot bills (HB 438 and HB 286) stall.
  • First Chatbot Bills of the Year Pass Out of Their Legislatures: Oregon’s SB 1546 and Washington’s HB 2225 have passed both chambers.
  • Three Additional Bills Pass Both Chambers: New York’s A 3411B (genAI), Virginia’s HB 797 (transparency), and Washington’s HB 1170 (genAI/ transparency).
  • Four Bills Pass First Chamber: Georgia’s SB 540 (chatbots), Hawaii’s HB 1782 (chatbots), HB 2458 (data-driven pricing), and SB 3001 (mental health chatbots).

 

Stuff from the States

 

California - Generative AI Law Constitutionally Upheld: A federal judge denied xAI’s preliminary injunction motion to block enforcement of AB 2013 (effective Jan. 2026), finding that the law likely does not violate the First Amendment. The court ruled that the law’s requirement for generative AI developers to publicly disclose training dataset information likely implicated a content-based regulation of commercial speech, subject to the intermediate scrutiny standard. Applying the Central Hudson test, the court held the state’s interest in factual transparency was substantial and the disclosure requirements not more extensive than necessary (despite acknowledging it was possible but not likely as required for granting a preliminary injunction).

 

Colorado -  Health Bill Passes Committee - HB 1195 (an Illinois’ HB 1806-style bill) passed in committee.

 

Connecticut - ADMT/ Employment - SB 435: Introduced by the Joint Committee on Labor and Public Employees, this bill would require disclosures to applicants and employees when ADS are used in employment, mandate human review for final employment decisions, and require annual independent bias audits. Employers would also be required to provide individuals with access to relevant data, opportunities to correct errors, and the ability to appeal adverse decisions involving ADS. The bill would additionally clarify that discriminatory outcomes from automated systems may constitute violations of state anti-discrimination law. 

 

Delaware - Transparency Bill to Address Chatbots and AI Agents Passes Committee- HB 306: Introduced by Rep. Romer (D), this bill would require businesses to clearly disclose when consumers are interacting with a chatbot, AI agent, or avatar during commercial transactions. The bill includes a private right of action. The bill subsequently passed through committee after its introduction this week. Notably, while not defined in the bill, the text references AI agents alongside chatbots and avatars, one of the first instances of the term appearing directly in legislation.

 

Georgia - Chatbot Bill Passes First Chamber: SB 540 would require operators of “conversational AI services” to provide nonhuman disclosures to minors every three hours and restrict engagement optimization. Among other requirements, this bill would require age verification before allowing access to a chatbot that could provide sexually explicit synthetic content. Operators would also be required to offer tools for parents to manage minors’ privacy and account settings and be prohibited from “knowingly or intentionally” causing or programming a chatbot designed to provide professional mental or behavioral health care.

 

Hawaii - Multiple bills passed first chamber: 

  • Companion Chatbots - HB 1782: This bill, requiring certain safeguards for minors, was amended to add definitions such as crisis intervention and emotional dependency. 
  • Data-Driven Pricing - HB 2458: This bill, prohibiting data-driven pricing in food sales, was amended to remove specific references to loyalty programs, specify each violation is a separate cause of action, and define “personally identifiable information.” 
  • Mental Health Chatbot - SB 3001: This bill, mandating chatbot mental health protocols, was amended to extend the disclosure requirements to every three hours (previously every hour), limit the safety protocols to suicidal ideation, and add data privacy protections. 

 

Kentucky - Youth Online Safety Bill Removes Chatbot Provisions - HB 227: This bill has been amended and no longer includes provisions regulating AI companion chatbots, only focusing on youth online safety requirements for social media platforms.

 

Minnesota - Data-Driven Pricing/ Employment - HF 4131 / SF 4280:  Introduced by Rep. Greenman (D), this bill would prohibit the use of surveillance-based data to inform individualized pricing or wage decisions through automated decision systems. Exceptions would allow differential pricing or wages when justified by actual cost differences, part of transparent and broadly available discount programs, or (for insurers) based solely on risk-relevant data. 

 

Mississippi - AI Definition Bill Signed by Governor - HB 1723 was signed by Governor Reeves (R). The measure adds a definition of “artificial intelligence” to Mississippi code, largely modeled on the OECD’s AI definition.

 

New Hampshire - Two bills passed committee:

  • Right to Compute - HB 1124: The bill would establish a right to compute, similar to enacted Montana SB 212.
  • Health - SB 640: This bill would prohibit the use of AI to deliver any service that requires a professional license unless the service is provided by a licensed practitioner.

 

New York - 

  • Legislator Addresses AI-Powered Toys - S 9408: Introduced by Sen. Gounardes (D), one of the authors of last year’s RAISE Act on frontier models, this bill would prohibit the manufacture and sale of AI-powered chatbot toys for children under thirteen in New York for five years. The bill would also mandate a comprehensive interagency study on the risks and benefits of chatbot toys to child users, including discussion on the data collection and retention practices of the toys. This bill follows the introduction of California’s SB 867, which would impose a similar prohibition on AI-powered chatbot toys, and Maryland’s HB 1261, which would establish child safety, data privacy, and oversight requirements for AI-enabled toys.
  • GenAI Transparency Bill Passes Both Chambers - A 3411B: This bill would require operators of GenAI systems to display a notice on a system’s interface that the GenAI outputs may be inaccurate. Failure to provide the notice would result in a civil penalty up to $1,000 per violation.

 

Oregon - Chatbot Bill Prepares to Be Sent to the Governor: SB 1546 passed the legislature and is poised to be sent to the Governor. Once the bill is transmitted, the Governor will have five business days for signature. The bill would establish a companion chatbot framework similar to California’s SB 243, with some additional requirements. Like, CA SB 243, it would create a private right of action for injured parties.Under the bill, an “artificial intelligence companion” is defined as a system designed to simulate a sustained human-like relationship with a user through personalized interactions and ongoing dialogue about personal or emotional topics; however, the definition explicitly excludes software used solely for customer service, education, financial services, healthcare support, business productivity, or technical assistance. If signed, the bill will require: 

  • Clear and conspicuous disclosures to users; 
  • Mandated safety protocols, including referrals to crisis resources when users express self-harm ideation;
  • Additional protections for minors, such as preventing the generation of content that simulates emotional dependence on the user or simulates romantic interest;
  • Prohibitions against engagement-maximization or reward mechanisms directed at minors (not included in CA SB 243).

 

Tennessee - 

  • Bill Establishing “Coercive Suicide” Offense Removes AI Provision- SB 1815: This bill would define the term “coercive suicide” (advising or encouraging another person to attempt to commit suicide) and previously would have clarified when an entity owning an AI system would commit this offense. The bill passed through its first chamber but was amended to remove any references to AI systems.
  • Chatbot Bill Amended and Passed Committee - SB 1700: Introduced by Sen. Akbari (D), this bill was amended in committee to require a study on the potential regulation of AI systems and genAI chatbots in this state. Previously, the bill would have set a series of safety and disclosure requirements for companion chatbots.

 

Utah - Utah’s Legislative Session Closes With Three Additional Bills Sent to the Governor:

  • Health - SB 150 would establish a process within the state licensure board for medical professionals for expanding healthcare practitioner’s scope of practice that includes technological innovations (like AI).
  • GenAI - HB 276 would require large online platforms (>2 million monthly users) to detect, disclose, and preserve provenance data and provide user tools to inspect that information. 
  • Privacy/ADMT - HB 450 would update Utah's data privacy laws by introducing new definitions for automated decision making and profiling, including requiring the development of a data privacy framework that incorporates best practices for automated decision making. 
  • Chatbot (and Education Sandbox) Bills Stall in Legislature: Before the end of session, several major AI-related bills failed to advance, including two chatbot bills (HB 438 and HB 286), one of which also addressed frontier models, as well as a proposal that would have established an education AI regulatory sandbox program (SB 322). The outcome comes amid reported federal attention to HB 286 urging Utah lawmakers to reconsider the proposal, reflecting broader tensions over state-level AI regulation and federal engagement in these debates.

 

Vermont - Health and Chatbot Bill Passes Committee - H 814: This bill would mandate disclaimers for AI-generated patient communications, restrict advertising and data collection for mental health chatbots, and enumerate a list of “neurological rights”. The bill heads to the Appropriations Committee.

 

Virginia - Transparency Bill Amended and Passes Both Chambers - HB 797 was amended on the floor and now directs the Joint Commission on Technology and Science (JCOTS) to study the feasibility and impact of establishing a framework for independent verification organizations (IVOs) that would assess whether AI systems adhere to safety standards aimed at preventing personal injury or property damage. Prior to these amendments, the bill would have directly created a licensing framework for independent AI verification organizations.

 

Washington - Two bills passed the legislature: 

  • GenAI / Transparency - HB 1170: Amended in committee before passage, this bill would require covered providers to include provenance data in any content that is created or materially altered by the covered provider’s genAI system, with exclusions for video games. The bill would also require government agencies that make AI systems available to consumers to disclose that the consumers are interacting with an AI system, including provenance data.
  • Chatbots - HB 2225: This bill would require operators of AI companion chatbots to implement safeguards for users, including preventing sexually explicit or suggestive interactions and prohibiting manipulative engagement techniques designed to foster emotional dependence for minors. Similar to SB 243, it would also require users expressing suicidal ideation to be referred to a crisis hotline and public disclosure of the number of crisis referral notifications issued to users. The bill defines an AI companion chatbot as providing “adaptive, human-like responses” and sustaining an “ongoing relationship” with users across multiple interactions. Similar to SB 243, this definition excludes bots used solely for business operations or customer service, gaming-related chat features, voice assistants that do not sustain relationships. However, this bill includes an additional carve out for narrowly tailored educational tools used in instructional settings.

 

Upcoming Hearings

  • Colorado - HB 1210 (Data-Driven Pricing/Employment) is set to be heard March 12 in the House Business Affairs & Labor Committee.
  • Colorado - HB 1263 (Chatbots) is set to be heard March 19 in the House Business Affairs & Labor Committee.
  • Maryland - SB 889 (Data-Driven Pricing) and SB 827 (Chatbots) are set to be heard March 12 in the Senate Finance Committee.
  • Tennessee - HB 1468 (Data-Driven Pricing), HB 1898 (Frontier Models/ Chatbots), and HB 1946 (Chatbots) are set to be heard in the House Banking and Consumer Affairs Committee on March 18.

  • Tennessee - SB 2171 (Chatbots/Frontier Models) set to be heard in the Senate Judiciary on March 16.

 

Federal

 

NTIA Report on State AI Laws Delayed: An NTIA report identifying state AI laws deemed “onerous” originally expected on Wednesday under a December White House executive order has been delayed. The forthcoming report is expected to highlight decisions around BEAD non-deployment funding for states with AI regulations viewed as conflicting with federal policy.

 

What We Are Reading

 

The Compulsion Paradox and the Pentagon-Anthropic Spat: When "Deregulation" Means Dictating AI Design: A recent analysis from Jones Walker examines Anthropic’s lawsuit challenging the government’s use of the Defense Production Act to compel changes to its AI safety architecture, raising questions about whether a policy framed as deregulation can include ordering companies to modify their systems. The case could set precedent for how far the government can go in directing private AI development and whether “deregulation” can coexist with federal authority to compel changes to AI safety practices.

 

The Pro-Human AI Declaration: A new public statement from a broad coalition of researchers and advocates (e.g. American Federation of Teachers, AFL-CIO Tech Institute, Yoshua Bengio, Susan Rice, and many others) argues that AI development should focus on augmenting rather than replacing human roles. The statement outlines principles aimed at keeping humans in control of AI systems, preventing excessive concentration of technological power, protecting core human experiences, and ensuring accountability for AI developers.
